title: Malayalam Cinema's Two Hottest Directors Made a Film Together. It Just Played Cannes.
excerpt: Manjummel Boys' Chidambaram and Aavesham's Jithu Madhavan unite for Balan: The Boy — a psychological thriller releasing in five languages on June 19 that already has Suriya, Ajay Devgn, and Naga Chaitanya publicly backing it.
body:
There is a scene in the Balan: The Boy trailer where a woman introduces herself by one name, and then another, and then a third. She is running. Her son is with her. The police are closing in. And you have no idea what she did — or whether she did anything at all.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=cjWTqndgZ_M

That ambiguity is the point. Director Chidambaram, whose Manjummel Boys became 2024's most electrifying survival drama and one of the highest-grossing Malayalam films ever made, has clearly decided that his follow-up should be the opposite of a crowd-pleaser. Where Manjummel Boys was visceral and collective, Balan is intimate and unsettling — a psychological thriller built on paranoia, fractured identities, and a mother's ferocious will to protect.

The script comes from Jithu Madhavan, whose Aavesham — starring Fahadh Faasil in one of his most unhinged performances — was the other Malayalam sensation of 2024. Between them, Chidambaram and Madhavan represent everything that has made Kerala's film industry the most creatively fearless in India right now. Putting them together on one project is the kind of move that makes other industries nervous.

What the Trailer Reveals (and What It Doesn't)

The two-minute trailer keeps its cards infuriatingly close. A mother and her young son appear to be on the run. She cycles through identities — Mary Luca, Sherly, possibly others. A grandmother figure enters the picture, and the word "violent" barely covers what her presence suggests. There are flashes of conflict, whispered accusations, and a child who watches everything with eyes that know too much.

Sushin Shyam — the composer behind the scores of Manjummel Boys, Kumbalangi Nights, and Minnal Murali — handles the music, which in the trailer alone swings between eerie ambience and something that sounds like a lullaby fed through a nightmare. Cinematographer Shyju Khalid (Premam, Kumbalangi Nights) frames everything in tight, anxious compositions that leave you searching the edges of the screen.

The cast is led by Chandu Salimkumar, with Farzana Palathingal, Dolly June, and Jean Paul Lal rounding out an ensemble that avoids star power in favour of faces that feel startlingly real.

The Cannes Card

Before Indian audiences had seen a single frame, Balan: The Boy was already generating conversation overseas. The film was screened at the Marché du Film during the Cannes Film Festival 2026, where it reportedly drew a strong response from international buyers and festival programmers. For a Malayalam-language psychological thriller starring no A-listers, that's a statement.

The Cannes showcase also explains the remarkable support the film has received from across the industry. Ajay Devgn, Suriya, Naga Chaitanya, and Raj B. Shetty have all publicly shared the trailer and extended their backing — an unusual show of cross-industry solidarity that suggests the film's reputation preceded its marketing.

Five Languages, One Bet

Balan: The Boy releases theatrically on June 19 in Malayalam, Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, and Kannada — a five-language simultaneous release that signals massive confidence from producers KVN Productions and Thespian Films. The multilingual push is no accident. After Manjummel Boys proved that Malayalam films could travel to Hindi-speaking audiences with the right story, and after RRR and Pushpa shattered the idea that pan-India meant only Telugu blockbusters, the playbook has changed.

For diaspora audiences, this is particularly significant. Five languages mean the film will land on screens across North America, the UK, and the Middle East with minimal delay and maximum accessibility. Whether your family watches in Malayalam at home or your Telugu-speaking roommate wants to tag along, the barrier is gone. This accessibility is crucial for maintaining cultural ties and ensuring that Indian narratives resonate with the diaspora, fostering a sense of community even from afar.

There is one note of caution: the Telugu dubbed trailer has drawn criticism for what viewers described as artificial, possibly AI-generated dubbing. If the theatrical release carries the same quality, it could undermine the film's pan-India ambitions in a market that has shown zero tolerance for lazy localisation.

Why This Matters

Malayalam cinema in 2024-2026 has been on a run that no other Indian film industry can match for consistency. Manjummel Boys, Aavesham, Premalu, Bramayugam, Aadujeevitham — the hits keep coming, and they keep being the kind of films that make you rethink what commercial Indian cinema can look like. Balan: The Boy could be the next chapter in that story, or it could be the first sign that the golden run is slowing down.

Either way, when the directors of Manjummel Boys and Aavesham make a film together, you show up. June 19. Five languages. No excuses.
